Abstract 19

We present bulk-rock and mineral Fe isotope data of ultramafic to mafic xenoliths and basaltic to 20

andesitic lavas from Adagdak Volcano (Adak Island, Central Aleutians) to study the effects of 21

early differentiation on the Fe isotopic evolution of island arc basalts and their crystallization 22

products. The Fe isotope composition of ultramafic cumulate xenoliths increases from dunite 23

(δ56Fe = –0.09 to –0.02‰) to clinopyroxenite (δ56Fe = +0.06 to +0.09‰), consistent with higher 24

modal proportions of clinopyroxene (δ56Fe = –0.05 to +0.11‰) relative to olivine (δ56Fe = –0.10 25

to +0.06‰) in the latter. Mid-crustal cumulate amphibole gabbro and hornblendite cumulates 26

also record heavier Fe isotope compositions (δ56Fe = +0.04 to +0.08‰) due to the abundance of 27

isotopically heavy amphibole (δ56Fe = +0.07 to +0.09‰) and magnetite (δ56Fe = +0.11 to 28

+0.13‰) in these rocks. High inter-mineral fractionations observed in spinel-olivine and spinel- 29

clinopyroxene pairs (Δ56Fespl-ol = +0.12 to +0.28 and Δ56Fespl-cpx = +0.06 to +0.19) suggest that 30

spinel is not recording equilibrium crystallization conditions for the ultramafic assemblages, 31

likely due to subsolidus Fe-Mg exchange. Our data also include Fe isotope measurements of one 32

1. Introduction 56

Iron isotope variations in lavas and mantle rocks are effective tracers of differentiation (Sossi et 57

al., 2012; Nebel et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2018), partial melting (Weyer and Ionov, 2007; 58

Williams and Bizimis, 2014), and changes in oxygen fugacity (fO2) (Williams et al., 2005; 59

Dauphas et al., 2014). The utility of Fe isotopes (expressed in delta notation as δ56Fe = 1000 × 60

[(56Fe/54Fe)sample/(56Fe/54Fe)standard –1)] in understanding these processes largely reflects the 61

respective affinities of isotopically light versus heavy Fe for reduced (Fe2+) and oxidized (Fe3+) 62

valence states (Polyakov and Mineev, 2000). Due to the oxidized nature of arc lavas (up to 3 log 63

units above the fayalite-magnetite-quartz redox buffer [FMQ]) relative to mid-ocean ridge 64

basalts (MORB: ~FMQ) (e.g., Cottrell et al., 2021, and references therein), and the preference 65

for isotopically heavy Fe species in oxidized magmas (Dauphas et al., 2009, 2014; Roskosz et 66

al., 2023), arc magmas are theoretically expected to display higher δ56Fe than MORB. However, 67

the Fe isotope compositions of arc lavas show more variability and extend to isotopically lighter 68

values than the observed range in MORB (arcs: δ56Fe = –0.09 to +0.20‰, Dauphas et al., 2009; 69

Foden et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2023; as compared to MORB: δ56Fe = 70

+0.06 to +0.18‰, Weyer and Ionov, 2007; Teng et al., 2013) (Fig. 1a). 71

The greater variability in δ56Fe and the presence of isotopically light compositions in arc 72

lavas may reflect a combination of several processes that distinctively operate in subduction 73

zones, including (1) greater depletion in some arc sources due to higher extents of wet melting 74

(e.g., Nebel et al., 2015; Foden et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021), (2) reaction between subarc 75

mantle peridotite and isotopically variable fluid fluxes from the subducted slab (Nebel et al., 76

2013; Debret et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023), or (3) the effects of lower to mid- 77

crustal differentiation in arcs (Li et al., 2020; Cooper and Inglis, 2022; Du et al., 2022). For 78


<!-- Page 4 -->


example, subarc mantle peridotites are also isotopically light relative to those from mid-ocean 79

ridges (Fig. 1b and references therein), which may reflect prior melt depletion of the subarc 80

mantle (Williams et al., 2005; Williams and Bizimis, 2014) or metasomatism by isotopically 81

light fluids derived from serpentinite breakdown in the slab (Debret et al., 2016, 2018, 2020). 82

The latter process would suggest that the δ56Fe of arc magmas may be inherited from their 83

sources. In contrast, Foden et al. (2018) observed negative correlations between arc thermal 84

parameter (φ, an expression of the slab temperature profile) and δ56Fe in a globally distributed 85

suite of mafic arc lavas, suggesting that light Fe isotope compositions in convergent margin 86

magmas may instead reflect greater extents of flux melting in arcs with older and colder 87

subducting slabs. This would imply that the isotopic depletion in some arc magmas reflects not 88

only variable degrees of alteration of the mantle source but also differences in geodynamic 89

regime. 90

In concert with the above processes, magmatic differentiation may also play an important 91

role in the Fe isotope evolution of arc magmas due to the differences in bond strength between 92

fractionating minerals (including silicates, oxides, and sulfides) and the melt (Dauphas et al., 93

2014; Sossi and O’Neill, 2017). Isotopically heavy Fe is preferentially incorporated into Fe3+- 94

bearing phases (e.g., oxides such as magnetite) over Fe2+-bearing phases (e.g., olivine, 95

orthopyroxene, garnet, and sulfides). The effects of magmatic differentiation on Fe isotope 96

systematics in arcs have primarily been studied through the volcanic record (Nebel et al., 2015; 97

He et al., 2017; Foden et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2023). For example, 98

Williams et al. (2018) found that producing the major/trace element and Fe isotope trajectories 99

(δ56Fe = –0.04 to +0.09‰) of basaltic to dacitic lavas from Anatahan volcano (Marianas) 100

requires three distinct stages with different crystallizing assemblages, including (1) olivine and 101


<!-- Page 5 -->


pyroxene, (2) magnetite, and (3) sulfide fractionation. In comparison to the Marianas, which are 102

built on relatively thin crust (~20 km; Calvert et al., 2008), the Fe isotope compositions of lavas 103

from the Central Andes have higher δ56Fe (+0.14 ± 0.04‰) and Sm/Yb (Du et al., 2022). This 104

may suggest that early garnet fractionation at the base of the thick Andean crust (~60 km) drove 105

later-stage melts to heavier Fe isotope compositions (Du et al., 2022). However, in a recent study 106

of Indonesian calc-alkaline lavas, Johnson et al. (2023) found no correlations between indices of 107

fractionation (e.g., SiO2 and MgO) and δ56Fe. This led the authors to suggest that δ56Fe of the 108

melt was buffered by the crystallization of isotopically heavy magnetite, which prevented late- 109

stage magmas from acquiring heavy Fe isotope compositions (Johnson et al., 2023). Taken 110

together, these studies suggest that fractional crystallization may have variable effects on the Fe 111

isotope evolution of magmas depending on the crystallizing assemblage and P-T-fO2-H2O 112

conditions. 113

The plutonic record of differentiation in arcs and its effect on Fe isotope systematics in 114

evolving melts has received comparatively less attention. Li et al. (2020) measured the Fe 115

isotope compositions of gabbro and diorite samples from the Tongde region of Southern China. 116

These rocks display an initial period of modest isotopic enrichment followed by a decrease in 117

δ56Fe as fractionation progresses, a pattern which Li et al. (2020) attribute to the removal of 118

isotopically light garnet, pyroxene, and olivine in a deep crustal hot zone followed by 119

crystallization of isotopically heavy amphibole at mid-crustal levels. Cooper and Inglis (2022) 120

found that mid to upper-crustal (≤ 0.4 GPa) gabbro, gabbronorite, and hornblendite cumulate 121

xenoliths from the Lesser Antilles had higher δ56Fe compositions than upper-crustal non- 122

cumulate gabbro xenoliths and erupted lavas, suggesting that mid-crustal fractionation depleted 123

the melt in the heavy isotopes of Fe. However, this cumulate suite was restricted to mid to upper- 124


<!-- Page 6 -->


crustal samples (≤ 15 km; Cooper et al., 2016, 2019) and did not include lower crustal ultramafic 125

assemblages (MgO <13.4 wt.% for all samples analyzed). 126

Understanding the source of the Fe isotope variability in arc lavas requires constraining 127

the nature of primitive arc melts and how their δ56Fe evolves during ascent through the entire 128

crustal column. To address this, we measured Fe isotope compositions in ultramafic to mafic 129

cumulate (n = 28) and mantle (n = 1) xenoliths from a well-documented lower to mid-crustal 130

xenolith suite from the Adagdak Volcano on Adak Island, Central Aleutians (Fig. 2) (Debari et 131

al., 1987; Sosa et al., 2023). We analyzed both minerals (spinel, clinopyroxene, olivine, 132

amphibole, and magnetite) and whole-rock Fe isotope ratios. Amphibole Fe isotope data are 133

complemented by single-crystal synchrotron Mössbauer spectroscopy of two amphibole grains, 134

one from an amphibole gabbro (sample ADG-CB-1) and the other from a hornblendite (sample 135

ADG-82-18). These measurements allow us to determine Fe3+/ΣFe ratios for these grains and 136

evaluate the potential of amphibole to drive the Fe isotopic evolution of Adagdak melts. 137

Our data extend to more primitive compositions than reported in the previous study of 138

cumulate xenoliths (Cooper and Inglis, 2022), capturing a different, but complementary, interval 139

of fractional crystallization (Fig. 3). We also measured δ56Fe for five lavas from Mt. Adagdak, 140

ranging from basalt to andesite (Kay and Kay, 1985, 1990, 1994). With this data, we construct a 141

model to explore the effects of fractional crystallization of the isotopic evolution of arc magmas. 142

Our results show that the cumulates chronicle a complex isotopic history that is not captured in 143

the lava record. 144

2. Geological background and sample descriptions 145

The Aleutian oceanic arc spans approximately 2000 km, extending from the western edges of the 146

Alaskan Peninsula to its western terminus at the Kamchatka Peninsula. The arc consists of a 147


<!-- Page 7 -->


largely submarine intra-oceanic ridge, which is only subaerial at volcanic centers (e.g., Scholl et 148

al., 1975; Kay and Kay, 1994). Magmatism results from the northward subduction of the Pacific 149

plate beneath the North American plate (e.g., Jicha and Kay, 2018). Although the arc has 150

migrated northward since 40 Ma, active magmatism in the Aleutians has occurred in a geometry 151

similar to that of the present day for the past 52 to 46 million years (e.g., Kay et al., 1982, 1994; 152

Davis et al., 1989; Jicha et al., 2006; Jicha and Kay, 2018). Crustal thicknesses show little 153

variability and are approximately 39 ± 3 km all along the arc (Janiszewski et al., 2013). The 154

xenolith suite from Mount Adagdak on Adak Island in the central Aleutians was collected in the 155

late 1970s on the volcano’s western slope from an olivine-phyric basalt flow (Fig. 2) (Debari et 156

al., 1987). While the age of the Adagdak xenolith suite is unknown, exposed plutonic rocks on 157

Adak Island have been dated from ~14 to 38 Ma (Citron et al., 1980; Jicha et al., 2006; Kay et 158

al., 2019). The petrography, mineral chemistry, and crystallization conditions of the xenolith 159

suite are extensively described in Debari et al. (1987) and Sosa et al. (2023), but we briefly 160

highlight the most salient features here. 161

The samples described here were taken in 2017 from the Cornell collection, which 162

includes extensive xenolith suites from both Mount Adagdak and Mount Moffett on Adak Island. 163

The Adagdak xenolith suite is comprised of lower to mid-crustal cumulates, which range from 164

primitive spinel dunite and wehrlite to more evolved amphibole gabbro and hornblendite. The 165

crystallization sequence for the Adagdak cumulate suite is inferred to be olivine + clinopyroxene 166

+ spinel → clinopyroxene + amphibole + plagioclase + magnetite. The elongate and euhedral 167

character of amphibole in the amphibole gabbro and hornblendite samples suggests a cumulate 168

rather than peritectic origin (Debari et al., 1987; Sosa et al., 2023). peritectic amphibole is only 169

observed as thin veins (< 1% by volume) along clinopyroxene grain boundaries in (± olivine) 170


<!-- Page 8 -->


clinopyroxenite xenoliths (Sosa et al., 2023). The only oxide phase in the ultramafic cumulates is 171

Fe-Cr-Al-Mg spinel (hitherto referred to simply as “spinel”), while the amphibole gabbro and 172

hornblendite lithologies contain magnetite. The suite also contains one mantle lherzolite. 173

Olivine-spinel-pyroxene oxybarometry of the ultramafic lithologies yields oxygen fugacity 174

estimates of ΔFMQ = +0.1 to +2.1. Thermobarometry yields temperatures between 950 and 1150 175

°C for the ultramafic lithologies and 920 to 1070 °C for the amphibole gabbro and hornblendite 176

samples (Sosa et al., 2023). The dunite, wehrlite, and clinopyroxenite xenoliths display 177

adcumulate textures, whereas the amphibole gabbro and hornblendite samples have 178

mesocumulate to orthocumulate textures. Based on mineral chemistry, amphibole-only 179

geobarometry, and comparisons to experimental studies, Sosa et al. (2023) interpreted the 180

ultramafic assemblages (dunite and wehrlite cumulates) to be lower-crustal in origin, while the 181

more evolved amphibole gabbro and hornblendite cumulates are likely sourced from the middle 182

crust. 183

3. Materials and methods 198

3.1 Bulk-rock analyses 199

Samples were selected for bulk-rock analysis based both on grain size and the overall xenolith 200

dimensions to ensure a representative measurement. Samples were cut into smaller aliquots (40- 201

70 g per aliquot) to remove altered surfaces or veining. Samples were then polished with 202

sandpaper to remove any saw marks and sonicated in deionized water. Cleaned aliquots were 203

crushed and powdered in an agate grinding vessel. Powders were dried overnight at 110 ºC, then 204

heated to 1050 ºC for one hour to determine loss on ignition (LOI). The LOI for amphibole-rich 205

samples (n = 9) was performed at 1100 ºC to ensure any structurally bound water was 206

volatilized. Glass beads were prepared using a 10:1 mass ratio of Li-borate flux to sample 207

powder and fused at 1200 ºC. Major elements (Si, Ti, Al, Fe, Mn, Mg, Ca, Na, K, P) were 208

analyzed using a Panalytical Zetium 4 kW wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (XRF) 209

spectrometer at Caltech following methods in Bucholz and Spencer (2019). Trace elements (Cr, 210

Ni, Rb, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, Nb, Cs, all REEs, Hf, Ta, Pb, Th, U) were measured from glass chips of 211

the Li-borate beads through solution inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry following 212

methods described in Lewis et al. (2021). Bulk-rock xenolith compositions (n =19) are given in 213

the Supplemental Data (Table S2). 214

5.1 Effects of dehydrogenation on Fe3+/ΣFe in amphibole 418

Two lines of evidence suggest that cumulate amphibole experienced dehydrogenation after 419

crystallizing: 1) the presence of an oxo-component (O2– ) in amphibole gabbro ADG-CB-1 grain 420

6 (0.21-0.47 wt.%) and hornblendite ADG-82-18 grain 10 (0.49-0.71 wt.%; dependent on the 421

uncertainties of water concentrations), and 2) δD values (–16 to –52‰ for all measured grains) 422


<!-- Page 19 -->


that are heavier than the average reported measurements for arc magmatic waters as determined 423

from melt inclusions (–60 to –80‰; compilation in Ratschbacher et al., 2023) (e.g., Demény et 424

al., 2012). Dehydrogenation is accompanied by oxidation of ferrous to ferric Fe in the amphibole 425

structure through the following reaction: Fe2+ + OH– ⇌ Fe3+ + O2– + H+. Thus, the Fe3+/ΣFe 426

ratios determined by SMS of amphibole that has experienced dehydrogenation likely do not 427

reflect primary magmatic values. In an effort to estimate the magmatic Fe3+/ΣFe ratios of 428

amphibole during crystallization, we constructed two Rayleigh fractionation inverse models, 429

assuming an initial amphibole δD = –80‰ and H2O content of 2 wt.% (calculations and further 430

details given in the Supplemental Data). These calculations suggest that the Fe3+/ΣFe ratio of 431

ADG-CB-1 grain 6 and ADG-82-18 grain 10 during crystallization were 0.41 ± 0.04 and 0.30 ± 432

0.05, respectively. Due to its structural complexity, previous studies have not attempted to 433

rigorously constrain the amphibole force constant. Li et al. (2020) estimated an amphibole force 434

constant of 250 N/m based on the relationship between mineral coordination number and 435

Fe3+/ΣFe, as discussed by Sossi and O’Neill (2017), and assuming an amphibole Fe3+/ΣFe ratio of 436

0.53. Using the same method and a representative amphibole gabbro Fe3+/ΣFe ratio 0.41 ± 0.04, 437

we estimate an amphibole force constant of 241 ± 9 N/m for an average Adagdak amphibole 438

composition. 439

5.5 Mantle dunite 663

Subarc mantle peridotites display a wide range of Fe isotope compositions (56Fe = –0.37 to 664

+0.11‰), which extend to isotopically lighter values than are observed in mid-ocean ridge 665

(MOR) peridotite (Fig. 1, 56Fe = –0.09 to +0.11‰; Craddock et al., 2013; Sossi et al., 2016). 666

While Adagdak mantle dunite ADG-CB-9 (56Fe = –0.03 ± 0.05‰) falls within the range 667

observed for MOR peridotites, it is likely isotopically lighter than the MOR peridotite average of 668

+0.01 ± 0.01‰ (Craddock et al., 2013). Depletion in heavy Fe isotopes in arc peridotites may 669

reflect one or a combination of the following processes: (1) incompatible Fe3+ behavior during 670

partial melting, with the heavier isotopes of Fe preferentially being extracted from the residue 671

(Williams et al., 2004; Williams and Bizimis, 2014); (2) metasomatism from isotopically light 672

fluids or melts fluxed from the slab (Zhao et al., 2010, 2012; Poitrasson et al., 2013); or (3) 673

disequilibrium isotopic diffusion between melts and mantle wall rock during channelized ascent 674


<!-- Page 30 -->


(Weyer and Ionov; 2007; Teng et al. 2011; Foden et al. 2018; Turner et al., 2018). In this last 675

scenario, because light isotopes of Fe diffuse faster than heavy isotopes, disequilibrium 676

fractionation between percolating melts and mantle olivine results in a net transfer of isotopically 677

light Fe to the peridotite. 678

Previous studies have shown that partial melts of metamorphosed subducted forearc 679

material or possibly the subducted slab yielded important trace element contributions to the 680

parental magmas of Adak cumulates (Yogodzinski and Kelemen, 2007; Sosa et al., 2023) and 681

other plutonic rocks on Adak Island (Kay et al., 2019). Hence it is possible that the slight 682

isotopic depletion observed in lherzolite ADG-CB-9 stems from melt-rock reactions with partial 683

melts of altered oceanic crust (AOC) or subducted forearc material. The Fe isotope composition 684

of a component derived from the slab itself may be highly variable and would strongly depend 685

on where in the slab the contribution was sourced from and whether it took the form of a melt or 686

fluid. For example, hydrothermal fluids fluxed from the slab are isotopically light, and their 687

progressive removal during subduction should increase 56Fe in the remaining AOC (Rouxel et 688

al., 2003, 2008). Partial melting of this enriched source would be expected to produce 689

isotopically heavy melts, particularly if garnet remained in the residue, which would retain the 690

light isotopes of Fe (He et al., 2017; Sossi and O’Neill 2017). However, reduced fluids leached 691

from the slab may also precipitate veins of isotopically light secondary sulfides and Fe 692

oxyhydroxides (δ56Fe as low as –0.71‰ Rouxel et al., 2003) within the slab, creating regions 693

with highly depleted Fe isotope compositions. It is however unlikely that sediment subduction 694

significantly affected the Fe isotope composition of the mantle wedge beneath Adagdak, as 695

previous studies have shown subducted sediments to be isotopically heavy (56Fe = +0.05 to 696

+0.18‰, Nebel et al., 2015). The radiogenic isotope systematics of arc lavas globally are also 697


<!-- Page 31 -->


consistent with a small net transfer of subducted sediment to the subarc mantle (<4%, 698

Hawkesworth et al., 1993), particularly for the Central Aleutians (0.2-0.6% by mass sediment 699

transfer, Nielsen et al., 2016). 700

Regardless of whether the mantle dunite analyzed here experienced an isotopic depletion 701

or metasomatic event, the sample provides our best constraints on the Fe isotope systematics of 702

the subarc mantle beneath Adagdak. Using the mantle melting equations of Dauphas et al. 703

(2009), the calculated Fe isotope composition of magmas generated by 10% buffered fractional 704

melting at fO2 = FMQ +1 of our mantle dunite (δ56Fe = –0.03 ± 0.05‰) ranges from δ56Fe = – 705

0.08 to +0.02‰ (see Supplemental Data for a full discussion of modeling). This is consistent 706

with the previous study of Aleutian magmas by Foden et al. (2018), who report a δ56Fe value of 707

0.00 to +0.08‰ for Central Aleutian lavas. 708

While we cannot establish a direct petrogenic relationship between the cumulate xenoliths and 710

Adagdak lavas, we can use comparisons to experimental studies to evaluate whether the lavas 711

may represent a complement to the xenoliths over a given interval of differentiation. Cumulate 712

assemblages with similar mineral chemistry, modal proportions, and bulk compositions to the 713

Adagdak cumulate suite have been produced in experiments that fractionally crystallize primitive 714

hydrous basalts (H2Oinitial = 3-3.6 wt.%, Mg# = 67-76) at conditions relevant to the lower arc 715

crust (1-0.7 GPa, fO2 = NNO-NNO+2; Nandedkar et al., 2014; Ulmer et al., 2018). These 716

experiments produced melt compositions similar to our most primitive measured Adagdak basalt 717

(ADAG-81-4: 48.6 wt.% SiO2, Mg# = 49.6, Kay and Kay, 1994) after 40-55% crystallization of 718

olivine, clinopyroxene, and spinel, just before amphibole and magnetite saturated as cumulate 719

phases (Nandedkar et al., 2014; Ulmer et al., 2018). This suggests that the Adagdak basalts and 720


<!-- Page 32 -->


andesites measured here are capturing a complementary record of melt evolution to our more 721

evolved cumulate compositions (namely, the amphibole gabbro and hornblendite cumulates). 722

In contrast to the cumulate data, which show pronounced evolutionary trends, Fe isotope 723

compositions of the Adagdak lavas are all within error of each other (56Fe = +0.03 ± 0.02 to 724

+0.06 ± 0.02: Fig. 6a). While there are suggestions of slight positive correlations between 725

average 56Fe and indices of differentiation like MgO (Fig. 6a), the resolution on the data are not 726

suitable to assess whether the melts are in fact becoming isotopically lighter with decreasing 727

MgO. These data reveal fundamental issues with studying the Fe isotope systematics of lavas in 728

isolation. Mass balance dictates that 56Fe of the parental lavas should change gradually over 729

restricted melt fractions if the majority of Fe in the system remains in the melt during 730

crystallization. As our samples do not fully encompass the compositional diversity of all 731

Adagdak lavas (Fig. 6b), it is perhaps not surprising that over this restricted range in melt 732

composition (48.6 to 61 wt.% SiO2, 5.7 to 2.5 wt.% MgO), the Fe isotope composition of the 733

melt varies almost negligibly. The isotopic fractionation associated with crystallization and 734

magmatic evolution may, therefore, be more apparent in the cumulate record than in their 735

complementary lavas. The highly magnesian nature of the Adagdak dunite and wehrlite 736

cumulates also suggests that these samples crystallized from a primitive basalt (Mg# = ~66-76) 737

as compared to the more evolved lava compositions analyzed here (Debari et al., 1986; Sosa et 738

al., 2023). Our data also show that most primitive cumulates were isotopically light (56Fe = – 739

remaining melt. This implies that there was likely a period of enrichment in heavy Fe isotopes 741

To illustrate the effect that fractional crystallization can have on the Fe isotope systematics of arc 745

magmas, we use our Adagdak data to construct a mass balance fractionation model, in which our 746

bulk cumulate compositions are removed from a basaltic melt with an initial composition of 747

56Fe = 0.0‰. Note that changing 56Fe of the initial melt to any value within our predicted 748

range (δ56Fe = –0.03 to +0.05‰) merely serves to shift the isotopic composition of our modeled 749

melts and cumulates to isotopically lighter or heavier values and does not affect the degree of 750

predicted fractionation. The purpose of this model is to illustrate the complex isotopic evolution 751

magmas and their crystallization products may experience as fractionated assemblages change 752

from isotopically light dunite and wehrlite to heavier clinopyroxenite cumulates to isotopically 753

heavy amphibole+magnetite-bearing rocks. Our discussion below focuses on the most salient 754

features of this model and the insights it provides into the isotopic evolution of the Adagdak 755

cumulates and their parental melts. An additional detailed discussion of this modeling approach 756

and the parameters used is given in the Supplemental Data (Figures S12-S14, Tables S13-S15). 757

Roskosz et al. (2022) showed that the force constant of glasses with basaltic and andesitic 758

compositions is nearly a linear function of their Fe3+/ΣFe ratio. Although we do not know the 759

Fe3+/ΣFe ratio of the melts parental to the cumulates, we can approximate an appropriate value 760

based on fO2 estimates for the xenoliths themselves (Sosa et al., 2023). Oxygen fugacity 761

basalt, a temperature of 1050 °C, a pressure of 1 GPa, and an fO2 of FMQ+1, we used the 764

parametrization of Kress and Carmichael (1991) to estimate an appropriate Fe3+/ΣFe ratio for the 765

parental melts to the cumulates, which yielded a value of Fe3+/ΣFe = 0.22. The parameterization 766

of Roskosz et al. (2022) then yields an initial force constant of 230 N/m for our basaltic melt. 767

The major element evolution of the fractionating melt was modeled through stepwise 768

removal of representative bulk cumulate assemblages from a high-Mg basalt (Ulmer et al., 2018) 769

(Table S8). Based on these major element constraints, we constructed an isotope fractionation 770

model in which a primary mantle melt at fO2 = FMQ+1 with an initial Fe3+/ΣFe of 0.22 771

fractionates 10% dunite, 9% wehrlite, 7% olivine clinopyroxenite, 3% clinopyroxenite, and 20% 772

of an amphibole gabbro assemblage (Fig. 10). Representative whole-rock Fe3+/ΣFe ratios 773

estimated from the model proportions, chemistry, and density of minerals for each lithological 774

Banno (1973), and magnetite and spinel Fe3+/ΣFe ratios were calculated from EPMA data based 777

based on our Mössbauer data. Published and estimated Fe force constants for clinopyroxene, 779

al., 2023), these bulk force constants were used to calculate cumulate-melt fractionation factors 782

as each lithological group was fractionated from the melt. The representative whole-rock 783

compositions for each lithological group and temperature estimates used in modeling are given 784

in Table 3. 785

5.8 Implications for the Fe isotopic composition of the oceanic arc plutonic record 814

Our Fe isotope measurements of mineral separates show that different phases in the cumulate 815

sequence have strong and systematic affinities for isotopically heavy versus light Fe. This means 816

that the crystallization sequence and the proportions of specific phases fractionating from the 817

melt exert first-order controls on the isotopic composition of the bulk cumulate removed from 818

the magma, and by extension, the isotopic evolution of parental melts. Fractionation of 819

isotopically light dunite and wehrlite cumulates might produce an interval of increasing 56Fe in 820

primitive arc basalts, while the removal of isotopically heavy clinopyroxenite, hornblendite, and 821

amphibole gabbro assemblages results in depletion of heavy Fe isotopes in more evolved basalts 822

and andesites. Our data also imply the existence of (1) a lower crustal layer of low 56Fe (<0‰) 823

ultramafic cumulates (dunite and wehrlite) in the Aleutian arc crust and (2) a mid-crustal 824

reservoir of clinopyroxenite, hornblendite, and amphibole gabbro cumulates with higher 56Fe 825

(>0.05‰). 826

This is consistent with the previous study of Cooper et al. (2016), who found mid-crustal 827

amphibole+plagioclase-bearing cumulates from Statia, Lesser Antilles (56Fe = +0.09 to 828

+0.12‰), to be isotopically heavier than their complementary non-cumulate gabbros and lavas 829

(56Fe = +0.01 to +0.06‰), suggesting that fractionation of these isotopically heavy assemblages 830

depleted later stage melts in heavy Fe isotopes. Li et al. (2020) also argue that mid-crustal 831

amphibole fractionation played an important role in the isotopic evolution of intrusive rocks 832

from the Tongde region, South China, depleting the more evolved diorite compositions in the 833


<!-- Page 37 -->


heavy isotopes of Fe. If the plutonic non-cumulate rocks on Adak Island (namely the calc- 834

alkaline Hidden Bay pluton, Kay et al., 1990, 2019) are an upper crustal complement to the mid- 835

crustal cumulates (Sosa et al., 2023), and represent crystallized melts that have experienced 836

prolonged Fe isotope depletion from magnetite and amphibole fractionation, then we might also 837

suspect these rocks to be isotopically light relative to the amphibole gabbro and hornblendite 838

cumulates. Furthermore, our results suggest that for oxidized hydrous arc systems, amphibole— 839

independent of magnetite—may play a role in generating the depletion in heavy Fe isotopes 840

observed in erupted lavas (consistent with the conclusions of Li et al., 2020, and Cooper and 841

Inglis, 2022). 842

Our results also support previous studies that have suggested that amphibole may play a 843

key role in driving Fe-depletion trends in calc-alkaline magmas (Kay et al., 1991; Romick et al., 844

1992; Kay and Mpodozis, 2001; Walters et al., 2020; Barber et al., 2021; Du et al., 2022), with 845

the greatest proportion of the bulk Fe content for the hornblendite and amphibole gabbro 846

cumulates typically (90% of studied cumulates) hosted in amphibole (28-99% of the FeOT 847

budget) rather than in magnetite (0-46% of the FeOT budget) (Fig. 9). However, with regards to 848

Fe isotopes, the role of amphibole in dictating the trajectory of isotopic evolution might be 849

complicated by the fact that studies have shown amphibole Fe3+/ΣFe ratios to be highly variable 850

in arc systems (Fe3+/ΣFe = 0.14-0.64, Ratschbacher et al., 2023). Previous studies have shown 851

that oxidation state and Fe coordination number are equally important in governing the ability of 852

phases to accept heavy versus light isotopes of Fe, with minerals having higher Fe3+/ΣFe ratios 853

and lower Fe coordination numbers preferring the heavier isotopes (Roskosz et al., 2015; Sossi 854

and O’Neill, 2017; Nie et al., 2021). While garnet fractionation (which has been suggested to be 855

important in continental arcs with thicker crusts) should drive the remaining melt to higher 856


<!-- Page 38 -->


56Fe, and magnetite fractionation to lighter Fe isotope compositions, amphibole fractionation 857

may have the potential to drive arc melts Fe isotope compositions to lighter of heavier 56Fe 858

values depending on fO2 and amphibole Fe3+/ΣFe. Clinopyroxene might also play a dual role in 859

governing the Fe isotope trajectories of arc melts, as Mössbauer studies of mantle peridotites 860

have shown variable clinopyroxene Fe3+/ΣFe ratios (Fe3+/ΣFe = 0.05 to 0.37: Dyar et al., 1992; 861

Luth and Canil, 1993; Woodland, 2009; Hao et al., 2013). Given that amphibole and 862

clinopyroxene are both modally abundant phases in arc-related cumulates, our understanding of 863

the Fe isotope systematics of arc magmas would benefit greatly from future studies measuring 864

the force constants of amphibole and clinopyroxene with a range of Fe3+/ΣFe ratios. 865

Our findings do not contradict previous studies that have suggested that prior isotopic 866

depletion of the subarc mantle (Williams and Bizimis, 2014), oxygen fugacity (Williams et al., 867

2005; Dauphas et al., 2009), melt-peridotite reactions (Weyer and Ionov; 2007; Teng et al., 2011; 868

Foden et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2018) and mantle metasomatism (Chen et al., 2023; Debret et 869

al., 2016, 2018, 2020) exert strong controls over the Fe isotope systematics of arc magmas. 870

Indeed, the Fe isotope composition of primary arc melts will be a function of the initial 871

composition of the subarc mantle, temperature, and oxygen fugacity (Dauphas et al., 2009). 872

Instead, we argue that the diversity in Fe isotope compositions observed in arc lavas also reflects 873

important contributions from lower to mid-crustal fractionation, which act in concert with the 874

variations in source composition discussed by many previous authors. The light Fe isotope ratios 875

observed in many arc melts may also reflect fractionation of isotopically heavy magnetite and 876

amphibole. At high melt fraction, mass balance dictates that the effects of fractionation on the Fe 877

isotope composition of the crystallizing melt may be small if the majority of the system’s Fe 878

remains in the liquid. Cumulates may, therefore, also amplify trends towards lighter or heavier 879

Fe isotope ratios that may not be resolvable in the lava record. Robust characterization of the Fe 880

isotope dynamics in arcs requires integrating data from mantle residues, lavas, and cumulates for 881

individual systems. 882

6. Conclusions 884

Fully characterizing the isotopic evolution of arc magmatic systems requires constraining δ56Fe 885

for the subarc mantle, erupted lavas, and crustal cumulates. We have shown that lower to mid- 886

crustal cumulate xenoliths provide robust records of the Fe isotope systematics in evolving 887

magmas. Our results highlight the important role differentiation may play in the isotopic 888

evolution of arc systems. Fractionation of dunite and wehrlite cumulates may increase δ56Fe of a 889

differentiating melt, but once magnetite and amphibole saturation occur, removal of these 890

isotopically heavy phases will decrease δ56Fe in the melt. Only the latter interval of isotopic 891

evolution (when melt MgO is <6 wt.%) is captured by the Adagdak lava record, emphasizing the 892

importance of studying the complementary cumulate record. The light Fe isotope composition of 893

a unique mantle dunite xenolith indicates that the subarc mantle beneath Adak experienced some 894

depletion in heavy Fe isotopes, likely due to incompatible Fe3+ behavior during repeated 895

episodes of partial melting, or reactions between mantle peridotite and mantle/slab-derived melts 896

or fluids. Partial melting of this isotopically light mantle would have produced magmas with 897

light δ56Fe compositions, possible parental melts to the Adagdak dunite and wehrlite cumulates. 898

Our results highlight the importance of amphibole fractionation in influencing the Fe isotope 899

evolution of hydrous arc systems. As an isotopically heavy phase (56Fe = +0.07 to +0.09‰ in 900

Adagdak cumulates) and major Fe reservoir in mid to upper-crustal cumulate assemblages (26- 901

99% of the bulk FeOT budget for Adagdak amphibole gabbro and hornblendite cumulates), 902


<!-- Page 40 -->


amphibole fractionation may play an important role in explaining the depleted nature of some 903

erupted arc lavas relative to MORB. 904
